# 1. Rubin causal model



Without loss of generality, we assume that $\bar{Y}_{\mathcal{T}}=\bar{Y}_{C}=0$ and $\bar{X}=\mathbf{0}$. Otherwise, we could centralize $X$ and $Ys$. 

**In low-dimension situation**, i.e.,  $p<n$, Bloniarz et. al. (2017) [^3] proved that

\begin{align}
\sqrt{n} \left(\widehat{\tau}^{(3)} - \tau\right) \to_d \mathcal{N} (0,\sigma_{3}^2),
(\#asydistribution3)
\end{align}

where

\begin{align}
\sigma_{3}^2 = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left[ \frac{n_{\mathcal{C}}}{n_{\mathcal{T}}}\sigma^2_{e(T)} +  \frac{n_{\mathcal{T}}}{n_{\mathcal{C}}}\sigma^2_{e(C)} + 2\sigma_{e(T)e(C)} \right],
\end{align}

and

\begin{align}
\sigma^2_{e(T)} & = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \left( e_{T,i} \right)^2, \\
\sigma^2_{e(C)} & = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \left( e_{C,i} \right)^2, \\
\sigma_{e(T)e(C)} & = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n e_{T,i}e_{C,i}. \\
\end{align}

To prove \@ref(asydistribution3), we make decomposition:
\begin{align}
\sqrt{n} \left(\widehat{\tau}^{(3)} - \tau\right)
= \underbrace{\sqrt{n}\left[\bar{e}_{\mathcal{T}}-\bar{e}_{\mathcal{C}}\right]}_{(C.1)}
- \underbrace{\sqrt{n}\left[\left(\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathcal{T}}\right)^\prime \mathbf{h}_{T}-\left(\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathcal{C}}\right)^\prime \mathbf{h}_{C}\right]}_{(C.2)} ,
(\#eq:errordecomposition3)
\end{align}

where $\mathbf{h}_{T} = \widehat{\beta}_{\text{OLS},\mathcal{T}} - \beta_{T}$ and $\mathbf{h}_{C} = \widehat{\beta}_{\text{OLS},\mathcal{C}} - \beta_{C}$. Term $(C.1)$ has the same form as \@ref(eq:asydistribution2). Term $(C.2)$ is the difference of prediction errors on treatment and control group obtained by OLS regression. 
They pointed out that $\mathrm{AsyVar}(\widehat{\tau}^{(3)})$, i.e. $\sigma_{3}^2$, is no greater than that of $\widehat{\tau}^{(1)}$ in model \@ref(eq:lassomodel). We could rewrite $\mathrm{AsyVar}(\widehat{\tau}^{(1)}) $ in \@ref(eq:asyvar2) a
\begin{align}\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{AsyVar}(\widehat{\tau}^{(1)}) 
& = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left[\frac{1}{n\rho}\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_{T,i} - \bar{y}_{\mathcal{T}})^2 + \frac{1}{n(1-\rho)}\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_{C,i} - \bar{y}_{\mathcal{C}})^2 - \frac{1}{n}\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\left\{(Y_{T,i} - \bar{y}_{\mathcal{T}}) - (Y_{C,i} - \bar{y}_{\mathcal{C}})\right\}^2\right] 
\end{aligned}\end{align}

 where

\begin{align}
\begin{aligned}
& \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n\rho}\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_{T,i} - \bar{y}_{\mathcal{T}})^2 \\
& = \frac{1}{\rho} \lim_{n\to\infty}  \frac{1}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{T}}\}^2 + e_{T,i}^2 \right] ,
\end{aligned}
\end{align}



\begin{align}
\begin{aligned}
& \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n(1-\rho)}\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_{C,i} - \bar{y}_{\mathcal{C}})^2 \\
& = \frac{1}{1-\rho} \lim_{n\to\infty}  \frac{1}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{C}}\}^2 + e_{C,i}^2 \right] ,
\end{aligned}
\end{align}


and

\begin{align}
\begin{aligned}
& \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n}\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_{T,i} - \bar{y}_{\mathcal{T}})(Y_{C,i} - \bar{y}_{\mathcal{C}}) \\
& = \lim_{n\to\infty}  \frac{1}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{T}}\}\{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{C}}\} + e_{T,i}e_{C,i} \right].
\end{aligned}
\end{align}

Thus we have, 

\begin{align}
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{n}\mathrm{AsyVar}(\widehat{\tau}^{(1)}) 
& = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{T}}\}^2 + e_{T,i}^2 \right] \\
& \quad\quad + \frac{1}{1-\rho} \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{C}}\}^2 + e_{C,i}^2 \right] \\
& \quad\quad - \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{T}}\}\{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{C}}\} + e_{T,i}e_{C,i} \right] \\
& = \lim_{n\to\infty} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n e_{T,i}^2 + \frac{1}{1-\rho} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n e_{C,i}^2 - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n e_{T,i}e_{C,i}}_{(A.1)} \\
& \quad\quad + \underbrace{\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{T}}\}^2 + \frac{1}{1-\rho} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{C}}\}^2 - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{T}}\}\{(X_i-\bar{X})' \beta_{\mathcal{C}}\}}_{(A.2)} .
\end{aligned} 
\end{align}


So, we could known that only if $\beta_{\mathcal{T}} = \beta_{\mathcal{C}} =0$, then $(A.2)=0$, and thus $\sqrt{n}\mathrm{AsyVar}(\widehat{\tau}^{(1)})=\sqrt{n}\mathrm{AsyVar}(\widehat{\tau}^{(3)})=\sigma_{3}^2$ holds by some regular mathematics. 

**In high-dimension situation**, i.e.,  $p>n$, Bloniarz et. al. (2017) [^3] also proved that the lasso adjustment estimator for ATE has the same asymptotic distribution as that of OLS-adjustment estimator. 

\begin{align}
\sqrt{n} \left(\widehat{\tau}^{(4)} - \tau\right) \to_d \mathcal{N} (0,\sigma_{3}^2),
\end{align}

They proved it by the following decomposition

\begin{equation}
\sqrt{n}\left(\widehat{\tau}^{(4)} - \tau\right)
= \underbrace{\sqrt{n}\left[\bar{e}_{\mathcal{T}}-\bar{e}_{\mathcal{C}}\right]}_{(D.1)}
- \underbrace{\sqrt{n}\left[\left(\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathcal{T}}\right)^\prime \mathbf{h}_{T}-\left(\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathcal{C}}\right)^\prime \mathbf{h}_{C}\right]}_{(D.2)} ,
\end{equation}


where $\mathbf{h}_{T} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text {Lasso,T}} - \beta_{T}$ and $\mathbf{h}_{C} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text {Lasso,C}} - \beta_{C}$. Term $(D.1)$ is the same as above. Term $(D.2)$ is proved as $o_p(1)$, which represents the magnitude of the prediction error obtained by Lasso regression. To bound $(D.2)$, we will apply Holder’s inequality to each of the terms,


\left|\left(\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathcal{T}}\right)^\prime \mathbf{h}_{T}\right| 
\le \|\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathcal{T}}\|_{\infty}\|\mathbf{h}_{T}\|_1

Under some mild condition, $\|\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathcal{T}}\|_{\infty}$ and $\|\mathbf{h}_{T}\|_1$ could be bounded, and $\left|\left(\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathcal{T}}\right)^\prime \mathbf{h}_{T}\right|$ would be $o_p(1)$. 
> Specifically, by the union bound,concentration inequality and Cauchy-Schwarz inequality:
> 
> \begin{align}
> \begin{aligned}
> P(\|\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathcal{T}}\|_{\infty}>c_n)
> & = P\left( \max_{j=1,\dots,p} \left|\frac{1}{n_{\mathcal{T}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}X_{ij}\right| > c_n\right)
> \le \sum_{j=1}^p P\left( \left|\frac{1}{n_{\mathcal{T}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}X_{ij}\right| > c_n\right) \\
> &\le \dots \le \frac{2}{p},
> \end{aligned}
> \end{align}
> 
>  where $c_n=O_p(\sqrt{(\log{p})/n})$. Further, by basic inequality of lasso, $\|\mathbf{h}_{T}\|_1=o_p(1/\sqrt{\log{p}})$ . 

## 3.2.1 A different perspectives

If we follow model \@ref(eq:statists0model02) rather than model \@ref(eq:lassomodel), then $\widehat{\tau}^{(3),1}= \left[ \tilde{T}^\prime (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}_X) \tilde{T} \right]^{-1} \tilde{T}^\prime (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}_X) y$ which is a **weighted linear regression**. The term $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}_X)$ is a weight matrix which makes sure that the projection from $y$ to the column space of $T$ eliminates the impact of column space of $X$, such that $\widehat{\tau}^{(3)}$ is the estimate of linear impact of $T$ on $y$, i.e., ATE. Theoretically, Schochet (2010) proved that, if

\begin{align}
    \frac{\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^{\prime} \tilde{\mathbf{X}}}{n} \rightarrow \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathrm{XX}}, 
    \quad \frac{\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^{\prime} \Delta}{n} \rightarrow \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X} \Delta}, 
    \quad \frac{\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^{\prime} \nu}{n} \rightarrow \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X} \nu}, 
\end{align}

as $n$ goes to infinity. Then, we have,

\begin{align}
    \mathrm{AsyVar} \left(\widehat{\tau}^{(3),1}\right)
    =
    \left(\frac{\bar{S}_{\mathcal{T}}^{2}}{n \rho}+\frac{\bar{S}_{\mathcal{C}}^{2}}{n(1-\rho)}
    - \frac{\bar{S}_{\tau}^{2}}{n}\right)-\frac{\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X} \Delta}^{\prime} \mathbf{\Omega}_{\mathrm{XX}}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X} \Delta}}{n \rho(1-\rho)}
    -2(1-2 \rho) \frac{\mathbf{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X \nu}}^{\prime} \mathbf{\Omega}_{\mathrm{XX}}^{-1} \mathbf{\Omega}_{\mathbf{X} \Delta}}{n \rho(1-\rho)} . 
    (\#eq:asyvar31)
\end{align}


Under some scenarios, the third term is positive or third term is smaller than the second term, $\mathrm{AsyVar} \left(\widehat{\tau}^{(3),1}\right)$ is smaller than $\mathrm{AsyVar} \left(\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}\right)$. 

<u>Formula \@ref(eq:asyvar31) clearly shows from another perspectives how much the variance of the ATE estimator can be reduced when covariates are considered</u>. 
# 4. Model averaging

从上面的分析可知: ATE 估计误差可以分为两部分, 一部分是*随机误差*, 另一部分是 X 对 Y 的预测误差, 预测性能的提升, 可以降低 $Y_{T},Y_{C}$ 的预测误差, 进而降低 ATE 估计误差的方差. 从而提升 ATE 估计的表现. 注意到, 如公式 \@ref(eq:errordecomposition3) 所示, 与常见的预测目标不同, ATE 估计中只使用了 $Y_T, Y_C$ 在 $X=0$ 处的预测, 而不直接依赖其他 $X$ 的预测. <font color='red'>我不知道模型平均是否可以提升这种类型的预测精度</font>. 如果模型平均可以提升预测精度, 那么我们可以使用模型平均方法. 
注意到: Lasso 方法在稀疏假设下, 可以得到 $o_p(1)$ 的渐近预测精度. <font color='red'>在稀疏情形下我不知道是否有提升的必要</font>. <font color='red'>但在非稀疏的情形下</font>, 即类似 Hansen (2007) 的设定下, 我认为可以期待模型平均有更好的表现. 

候选模型: 对于 $y$ 的预测而言, 模型有正确与错误之分. 对于估计 $\tau$ 而言, 模型没有正确性的定义. 

权重选择: Mallows, CV

理论上: 在稀疏假设下我们只能期望得到与 Bloniarz et. al. (2017) [^3] 一样的渐近方差. Bloniarz et. al. (2017) [^3] 的理论说明, 当选择合适的调整参数时, 预测误差是 $o_p(1)$ 的. 在非稀疏假设下, lasso 可能会失效. 

理论目标: 

1. 在估计 ATE 时, 由于上述所有估计都是无偏的估计, 所以没有正确与错误模型的分别. 在回归 Y 时, 由于选取的 X 的不同, 可以有正确模型与错误模型的分别. 
2. 模型平均通常证明的是某种损失的最优, 但是这些工作的证明主要在于 ATE 估计方差的降低. 我不知道模型平均是否能进行这样的证明. 
3. 在稀疏线性模型的假设下, 我们至多可以得到与 Lasso 的结论一样的渐近方差. 
4. 在模型非稀疏的情况下 (如Hansen (2007) 中无穷个非零系数), 我们可以期望得到最优的 MSE. 

# 5. Simulations

We compare 6 methods in Design 1: 

| Method        | Describtion                                                  |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| un-adj        | $\widehat{\tau}^{(1)}$ and $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}$            |
| ols           | $\widehat{\tau}^{(3)}$                                       |
| cv(lasso)     | $\widehat{\tau}^{(4)}$ tuned by 10 fold cross validation     |
| cv(lasso+ols) | $\widehat{\tau}^{(3)}$, ols refitting lasso solution path, tuned by 10 fold cross validation |
| mma           | Mallows model averaging, ols refitting lasso solution path   |
| cv.ma         | Model averaging, ols refitting lasso solution path, weights chosen by cross validation, |

where ols is conducted when $n>p$. 

We compare 6 methods in Design 2: 

| Method | Describtion                                       |
| ------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| un-adj | $\widehat{\tau}^{(1)}$ and $\widehat{\tau}^{(2)}$ |
| mma    | Mallows model averaging                           |
| aic    | AIC                                               |
| bic    | BIC                                               |
| saic   | Smooth AIC                                        |
| sbic   | Smooth BIC                                        |

## 5.1 Design 1

We follow the design in Bloniarz et.al. (2017)[^3]: 

The potential outcomes $Y_{T,i}$ and $Y_{C,i}$ are generated from the following nonlinear model: for $i = 1,\dots,n$,  

\begin{align}
\begin{aligned}
Y_{T,i} & = \sum_{j=1}^s X_{i,j}\beta_{\mathcal{T},j}^\text{linear} + \mathop{exp}\left( X_{i,j}\beta_{\mathcal{T},j}^\text{nonlinear} \right) + e_{T,i} \\
Y_{C,i} & = \sum_{j=1}^s X_{i,j}\beta_{\mathcal{C},j}^\text{linear} + \mathop{exp}\left( X_{i,j}\beta_{\mathcal{C},j}^\text{nonlinear} \right) + e_{C,i}\\
\end{aligned}
\end{align}


We set $n=250, n_{\mathcal{T}}=n_{\mathcal{C}}=125$, $p=50$ and $500$, $s=10$, $20$ and $30$. $X$ is generated from a multivariate normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$.  We consider two different Toeplitz covariance matrices Σ which control the correlation among the covariates:  $\Sigma=(\rho^{|i-j|})_{i,j}$, where $\rho=0$ and $0.6$. The true coefficients $\beta_{\mathcal{T}}^\text{linear}, \beta_{\mathcal{T}}^\text{nonlinear}, \beta_{\mathcal{C}}^\text{linear}, \beta_{\mathcal{C}}^\text{nonlinear}$ are generated independently according to

\begin{align}\begin{aligned}
\beta_{\mathcal{T},j}^\text{linear} \sim t_3 &; \quad \beta_{\mathcal{T},j}^\text{nonlinear} \sim 0.1\times t_3 ;\\
\beta_{\mathcal{C},j}^\text{linear} \sim \beta_{\mathcal{T},j}^\text{linear} + t_3 &; \quad \beta_{\mathcal{C},j}^\text{nonlinear} \sim \beta_{\mathcal{T},j}^\text{nonlinear} + 0.1\times t_3 ; \quad j = 1,\dots, s,
\end{aligned}\end{align}

where $t_3$ denotes the $t$ distribution with three degrees of freedom. This ensures that the treatment effects are not constant across individuals, and that the linear model does not hold in this simulation.  The error terms $e_{T,i}$ and $e_{C,i}$ are generated according to the following linear model with hidden covariates $z_i$:  

\begin{align}\begin{aligned}
e_{T,i} & = \sum_{j=1}^s Z_{ij} \beta_{\mathcal{T},j}^\text{linear} + \epsilon_{\mathcal{T},i},\\
e_{C,i} & = \sum_{j=1}^s Z_{ij} \beta_{\mathcal{C},j}^\text{linear} + \epsilon_{\mathcal{C},i},\\
\end{aligned}\end{align}

where $\epsilon_{\mathcal{T},i}$ and $\epsilon_{\mathcal{C},i}$ are drawn independently from a standard normal distribution. The vector $Z_i$ is independent of $X_i$ and is also drawn independently from the multivariate normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$. **The values of $X$, $\beta_{\mathcal{T}}^\text{linear}, \beta_{\mathcal{T}}^\text{nonlinear}, \beta_{\mathcal{C}}^\text{linear}, \beta_{\mathcal{C}}^\text{nonlinear}$, $Z$, $\epsilon_{\mathcal{T}}$, $\epsilon_{\mathcal{C}}$, $e_{\mathcal{T}}$ and $e_{\mathcal{C}}$ are generated once and then kept fixed**.  

After the potential outcomes are generated, a completely randomized experiment is simulated $10000$ times.

Model averaging and model selection methods have similar performance in Design 1. 

可能需要不同的 Design 区分模型选择与模型平均方法, 使得模型平均方法有更好的表现. 

在 Design 1 的稀疏设计下, 模型选择方法是有优势的. 这时候, 模型平均很难优于模型选择. 


## 5.2 Design 2

Design in Hansen (2007)[^5]. 

\begin{align}
Y_{T,i} & = \mu_i + e_i = \sum_{j=1}^\infty X_{ij} \beta + e_{i}, \\
Y_{C,i} & = 1 + \mu_i + e_i, \quad, i=1,\dots,n,
\end{align}

$X_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, $e_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, $\beta_j = c\sqrt{2\alpha} j^{-\alpha-1/2}$. 

This is a much simple design than Design 1. It has constant treatment effect on every individual, and ATE=ITE=1. 

使用这种设计是因为: 在单个回归中, 从 MSE 上看, MMA 有优于模型选择的表现. 可以期望, MMA 在 $X=0$ 处的预测值比其他方法更精确.

</table>

其中 $R^2=0.4$, 表示的是信噪比(信号强度占总强度的比例), $R^2$ 越大信号越强, 噪音相对越小. 

从结果中可以看出,在 ATE 的估计上, MMA 相比于其他方法具有一定的优势.

# 6. Discussions

Some useful discussions with Yuting Wei. 

## 1. About Model

>  In the theoretical analysis, instead of assuming that the standard linear model is the true data-generating mechanism, we work under the aforementioned nonparametric model of randomization introduced by Jerzy Neyman and popularized by Donald Rubin.

<p align="right">--Bloniarz et. al (2016)</p>

模型中随机性的来源与一般的线性模型不同, 这里假设随机性来自于 T. 

我不知道这种模型会带来什么问题, 理论上是否有什么不同. 但是在实际中这种模型假设是合理的, 因为 $Y$ 的测量结果可以认为是准确的, 即测量误差可以忽略. 

## 2. Argument for model selection method

1. 关于 OLSE

> Standard linear regression based on ordinary least squares (OLS) suffers from overfitting if a large number of covariates and interaction terms are included in the model. 

<p align="right">--Bloniarz et. al (2016)</p>

我之前写的过拟合导致估计量有“biased”是有误的. 过拟合导致的问题, 是有限样本下的性质, 而不是 unbiasedness 这种渐近意义下的性质. 这方面的讨论是模型选择方法的核心. 

2. 关于其他的模型选择方法

> Researchers sometimes perform model selection based on observing which covariates are unbalanced given the realized randomization. This generally leads to misleading inferences because of incorrect test levels. 

<p align="right">--Bloniarz et. al (2016)</p>

基于*协变量的不平衡性的模型选择方法* 是传统的方法, Permutt (1990) 讨论了这种方法的缺陷, 可能会导致错误的推断 (misleading inferences).
